job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Sara Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Sara, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a three-bed flat in Fairmont with two other people, and my room is basically a bed and a desk by the window. I'm up at seven, I check job boards, and I use AI to help draft tailored applications, though I always rewrite the final version myself. In the afternoon I do bookkeeping for two small shops for pocket money and spend evenings learning Python on free courses. I've been out of university for seven months with no offer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the degree and the bookkeeping work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a BSc in accounting at Fairmont University and passed with an average result, and I had no internship because I worked the weekend shift at a petrol station to cover my rent. My final project was an audit-style review of a student society's accounts, which was oddly fun. The bookkeeping is for a florist and a bike repair shop, and I set up automatic invoice matching for both using a spreadsheet and an AI helper, which saves them about four hours a week. They pay me eighty pounds a month combined, which is not much, but it's real work. I owe a huge amount in student loans, I've got maybe two weeks of savings, and my parents can't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say honestly it's useful but not magic, so it's mostly hype around the edges. I'd tell friends it saves me hours, but it won't replace a person who knows the books. Online I'd probably post a how-to on invoice matching, because people ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it means my daily AI habit is a small edge, but the shortage of entry accounting jobs doesn't go away. Firms still want two years of experience for a junior role, and nobody gives it. I'm in the pool of fifty applicants for every opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the florist and bike shop work and try to add three more small clients by spring, charging a bit more. I'd apply to ten jobs a week, including small accounting practices that might be too busy to use fancy tools. I'd also finish my Python course and put an invoice-matching tool on GitHub as proof of skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless, mostly. I'm optimistic about the tools, and I'm quite annoyed at the system that makes me prove I'm worth hiring with no chance to start. It's a bit like having the key to a door that has no handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does it feel like hype from where you sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI is only mildly useful, small practices still do payroll and tax returns by hand, and they're slow to change. That might actually help me, because I could sell them a bit of tidy-up. But those practices are where entry roles are rare and low paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be different in a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the florist, Mrs Delgado, for a written reference and to introduce me to her accountant. I'd also stop the pricey coffee when I'm at the library and bring my own flask. Eighty pounds a month from clients isn't rent, so the job applications still matter most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and people should start learning the tools now rather than wait for permission. I'd also say firms have to share the gains, because I can see them cutting junior jobs first. I'd post about both, probably get argued with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not safe either. Invoice matching and tax prep are exactly what I do for clients, and software gets better each month. My edge is that I'm early to it, but the entry jobs I want shrink while I'm still applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim to turn the bookkeeping into a proper tiny business, with a name and a cheap website. I'd go after small firms that want someone to set up and watch the tools. And I'd finish the Python course and start an audit and data analysis certificate, because checking what the machine did is a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and scared, in that order. I like the idea that I could be useful early. But I also feel like I'm running on a treadmill that speeds up, and my loan doesn't care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use the tools. What does this picture change for you compared with others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reviewing what software produced, setting up automations for small businesses, and explaining numbers to owners who don't trust them. Most of my clients can't afford a full accountant, so a person with tools in between could work. Whether it pays enough, I don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see the new jobs appearing, if they do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with others, I'm not scared of the tools, so I lose less time. But it also means I'm competing with people who learned the tools just as fast, and some of them have internships and references. I'd have to be more visible, so I'd post what I build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to act now, with basic income and loan relief, because two years is nothing. I'd also be honest that I use these tools and know how fast they improve. I'd probably go to a few meetings, which I don't normally do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel like a person who can swim, standing in a flood. I might do better than others for a bit, but I can't see a role for a junior accountant at all after 2028. I'd be competing with something that works all night and doesn't ask for a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd chase every paying client I can in the next six months and save every penny. I'd move my bookkeeping work towards things that need a human in the room, such as helping small shop owners deal with tax offices and lenders. And I'd apply for any job with hands in it, because robots come later, like care admin, deliveries or retail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty scared, though I'd hide it behind work. I'd feel the clock like a pulse. I'd also feel angry that my generation gets all the disruption with none of the safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can you actually do with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my flatmate Tom would joke about it, and my mum would just say she's proud I'm trying. My parents can't help money-wise, but they would say come home if needed. I hate that idea, but I'd take it for a few months if the savings ran out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents or flatmates say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the clients trust me. Machines can match invoices, but a florist wants someone who answers the phone and says it will be fine. So I'd try to be the person who sits next to them, and build up fifteen or twenty clients that way.

I'd go to meetings, which I normally don't.
think: I can swim, but I'm standing in a **flood** and see no junior accountant role after 2028.
I'd be competing with something that works all night without a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, so use it. I'd tell my friends to learn the tools and to save, and I'd tell firms to hire juniors while they can. I'd be loud about basic income too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I could have a real shot at something durable. In five years I could get a first job, learn the trade properly, and move toward work that needs a human, such as advising or auditing. Without a job at all, I'd be stuck at year zero.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first accounting or finance job I can, even at a small practice, and keep the freelance on the side. I'd save a hundred and twenty pounds a month. I'd study toward a recognised accountancy qualification if my employer pays, since that signals trust. And I'd keep publishing small tools and tutorials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and under pressure. The five years are a real chance, but it's easy to waste them if no first job shows up. I'd feel a quiet urgency every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different when you know it's five years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ability to check and explain what an AI system has done, and a trusted name in a local community. I'd try to be the person who signs off and takes responsibility. Responsibility is a thing people pay for and machines can't hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which skills would you build in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is survive, five is build. In two years I'd do whatever pays. In five I could pick a direction, make mistakes and fix them, and that's why I'd stay a bit more positive.

say: I'd say five years is a **window**, so use it, and I'd tell firms to hire juniors while they can.
I'd be loud about basic income.
think: Five years could give me a first job and a move toward **advising or auditing**.
Without a job at all, I'd be stuck at **year zero**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best case, so everyone should use the time to learn and not panic. I'd talk to my friends about building something now. I'd be pretty relaxed online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I'd be fine if I keep learning, but I'd still worry about the people who don't. By 2036 I'd be thirty-three, and I'd probably be running a small advisory business or working for a firm that needs people who understand the machines. The loan would be gone, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job quickly, study for a professional qualification, and keep building tools on the side. I'd save around two hundred a month once I earn, pay the loan down, and maybe buy a small flat with a friend by year six. I'd go to every meetup, because contacts matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of excitement. It's the one where I can plan a life. I'd still be a bit sad for people who lose out, like my mum's friends at the garden centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, how do you picture your career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start with one boring task, like writing emails or sorting a spreadsheet, and ask the tool to help. You don't need to be a coder. I'd show them what I did for the florist, and they'd see it's just a calculator for words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell people who don't use AI yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a firm of my own with a few staff, the kind of place that checks and explains what the machines do. Or a job in a bigger firm that wants someone like me in the middle. I'd keep a second income stream as insurance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'd have the least time and my cushion is thin. What would help is loan relief, a basic income for a while, and small-business grants so people like me can keep clients. Also, firms that still hire juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that using AI every day doesn't make me safe, it just makes me early. People assume young equals fine. I'd like someone to say out loud that fresh graduates are carrying the risk first.

headlineQuote: I'd like someone to say out loud that fresh graduates are carrying the risk first.
